newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba, U.S. to continue bilateral immigration talks.
newsitem.headline: Cuba, U.S. to continue bilateral immigration talks.

text.p: Cuba and the United States will hold bilateral immigration talks next month in what will be the first official public contact between the two nations since the re-election of President Bill Clinton.
A Cuban Foreign Ministry official quoted by the Cuban news agency Prensa Latina said the talks would be held on Dec. 4 and 5 in Havana.

The conversations, which have been held periodically over the last two years, would continue to review the progress of immigration accords signed between the two countries in September 1994 and May 1995, the official said.

These accords, established following the so-called Cuban rafters' crisis of summer 1994, were aimed at stemming the flow of Cubans trying to enter the United States illegally by crossing the Florida Straits in flimsy boats and rafts.

They are a rare example of bilateral cooperation between communist-ruled Cuba and its superpower neighbour, whose relations have been characterised by hostility for more than three decades. The two nations do not have normal diplomatic ties and Washington maintains an economic embargo against Cuba.

Both sides have said they are generally satisfied with the way the immigration accords are being carried out, although Cuba has demanded the return of a number of Cuban nationals who hijacked planes to the United States.

Tensions between Washington and Havana increased sharply this year after Cuba shot down two small U.S. planes in February and the United States retaliated in March by introducing legislation aimed at curbing foreign investment on the island.
But the bilateral cooperation on immigration continued and U.S. authorities have returned to Cuba 482 Cubans intercepted at sea while trying to flee the island in the last 18 months.
The Cuban Foreign Ministry official cited by Prensa Latina did not indicate that any other item would be on the agenda of the December talks apart from immigration issues.

Cuba has said in the past it is willing to widen the dialogue to include the question of bilateral relations but the United States, which is pressing the Cuban government to adopt democratic reforms, has preferred to keep the periodic talks focused on immigration issues.
